body.en: Vectors model physical quantities possessing both magnitude and direction — such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force. Parametric equations decouple multi-dimensional trajectories by expressing spatial coordinates as explicit functions of an independent time parameter. This chapter formalizes Euclidean vector spaces, derives algebraic and geometric dot products, constructs orthogonal projections, develops the three-dimensional cross product and scalar triple product, and models linear and projectile kinematics.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Vector Algebra, Components & Unit Vector Normalization

body.en: Master component forms in 2D and 3D, compute Euclidean norms, perform scalar multiplication and vector addition, and normalize vectors into unit vectors.

caption.en: Coordinate grid showing geometric action of a linear transformation mapping △ABC to its image △A'B'C'.

body.en:
A vector \(\mathbf{v}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) or \(\mathbb{R}^3\) from initial point \(P(x_1, y_1, z_1)\) to terminal point \(Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)\) has standard component form: \[ \mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \rangle = \langle x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1, z_2 - z_1 \rangle = v_1\mathbf{i} + v_2\mathbf{j} + v_3\mathbf{k}. \]

Euclidean Norm (Magnitude): \[ \|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}. \]

Unit Vector Normalization: Any non-zero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) defines a unique collinear unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) of magnitude 1: \[ \hat{\mathbf{u}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \left\langle \frac{v_1}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}, \frac{v_2}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}, \frac{v_3}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} \right\rangle. \]

2D Direction Angle: In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{v}\|\langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \rangle\), where \(\theta = \text{atan2}(v_2, v_1)\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Vectors, Lines & Parametric Kinematics)

body.en:
Why Orthogonal Projection & Eigenvalue Characteristic Equations Work: Decompose \(\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\) where \(\mathbf{w} \perp \mathbf{v}\). Taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{v}\) uses \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) to isolate \(c\):

\[ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + 0 \implies c = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2} \]

For eigenvalues, \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) is equivalent to \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\). A homogeneous linear system has a non-trivial nullspace vector \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) if and only if the matrix \(A - \lambda I\) is singular, yielding the characteristic polynomial \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\).

label.en: Level 1 (Foundations) — Vector Resultant, Direction Angle & Unit Vector

problem.en: Given vectors \(\mathbf{u} = \langle 3, -4 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \langle -7, 1 \rangle\): (a) Find the resultant vector \(\mathbf{w} = 2\mathbf{u} - 3\mathbf{v}\). (b) Compute the magnitude \(\|\mathbf{w}\|\). (c) Find a unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{w}\).

solution.en:
(a) Resultant linear combination: \[ \mathbf{w} = 2\langle 3, -4 \rangle - 3\langle -7, 1 \rangle = \langle 6, -8 \rangle - \langle -21, 3 \rangle = \langle 6 - (-21), -8 - 3 \rangle = \langle 27, -11 \rangle. \]

(b) Magnitude: \[ \|\mathbf{w}\| = \sqrt{27^2 + (-11)^2} = \sqrt{729 + 121} = \sqrt{850} = 5\sqrt{34} \approx 29.15. \]

(c) Unit vector: \[ \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|} = \frac{1}{5\sqrt{34}}\langle 27, -11 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{27}{5\sqrt{34}}, -\frac{11}{5\sqrt{34}} \right\rangle. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Analytical Application — Dot Product Equivalence & Orthogonal Projections

body.en: Rigorously prove the equivalence of algebraic and geometric dot products using the Law of Cosines, decompose vectors into parallel and orthogonal components, and analyze motion using the projection explorer.

label.en: ● Dot Product Equivalence Theorem & Law of Cosines Proof

body.en:
Theorem: For non-zero vectors \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) with included angle \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\): \[ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3 = \|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\| \cos\theta. \]

Rigorous Proof: Form the triangle with vector sides \(\mathbf{u}\), \(\mathbf{v}\), and \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\). By the geometric Law of Cosines: \[ \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - 2\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta. \] Expanding the algebraic dot product of \(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\) with itself: \[ \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 = (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) \cdot (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u} - 2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 - 2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2. \] Equating the two expressions: \[ \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 - 2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - 2\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta. \] Subtracting \(\|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2\) and dividing by \(-2\) yields \[ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\| \cos\theta. \quad \blacksquare \]

Orthogonality Criterion: Two non-zero vectors \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are orthogonal (\(\theta = \pi/2\)) if and only if \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\).

Vector Projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\): \[ \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2}\right)\mathbf{v}. \]

Scalar Component (Signed Length): \[ \text{comp}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\cos\theta. \]

Orthogonal Decomposition: Every vector \(\mathbf{u}\) decomposes uniquely into a component parallel to \(\mathbf{v}\) and a component perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}\): \[ \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_\parallel + \mathbf{u}_\perp = \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}), \quad \text{where } \mathbf{u}_\perp \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0. \]

label.en: Level 2 (Analytical Application) — Orthogonal Decomposition in Force Physics

problem.en: A force vector \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 50, 120 \rangle\text{ N}\) acts on an object sliding along a ramp directed along \(\mathbf{v} = \langle 4, 3 \rangle\). Decompose \(\mathbf{F}\) into a component parallel to the ramp \(\mathbf{F}_\parallel\) (work-producing force) and a component normal to the ramp \(\mathbf{F}_\perp\) (normal force).

solution.en:
Step 1: Compute dot product and magnitude squared: \[ \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (50)(4) + (120)(3) = 200 + 360 = 560\text{ N}. \] \[ \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 16 + 9 = 25. \]

Step 2: Compute parallel projection \(\mathbf{F}_\parallel\): \[ \mathbf{F}_\parallel = \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{F} = \left(\frac{560}{25}\right)\langle 4, 3 \rangle = 22.4\langle 4, 3 \rangle = \langle 89.6, 67.2 \rangle\text{ N}. \]

Step 3: Compute perpendicular component \(\mathbf{F}_\perp\): \[ \mathbf{F}_\perp = \mathbf{F} - \mathbf{F}_\parallel = \langle 50 - 89.6, 120 - 67.2 \rangle = \langle -39.6, 52.8 \rangle\text{ N}. \]

Verification: \[ \mathbf{F}_\perp \cdot \mathbf{v} = (-39.6)(4) + (52.8)(3) = -158.4 + 158.4 = 0. \quad \checkmark \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor — 3D Cross Product, Scalar Triple Product & Equations of Planes

body.en: Construct the vector cross product in three dimensions, compute spatial areas and volumes via scalar triple products, and formulate vector equations of 3D lines and planes.

Definition: For vectors \(\mathbf{u} = \langle u_1, u_2, u_3 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \rangle\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the cross product is the vector: \[ \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix} = (u_2v_3 - u_3v_2)\mathbf{i} - (u_1v_3 - u_3v_1)\mathbf{j} + (u_1v_2 - u_2v_1)\mathbf{k}. \]

Geometric Properties:

  • Orthogonality: \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\) is mutually perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) (right-hand rule).
  • Parallelogram Area: \(\|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\| = \|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta\).
  • Anti-Commutativity: \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = -(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u})\).
  • Collinearity: Non-zero \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are parallel if and only if \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\).

label.en: ● Scalar Triple Product & Equation of a Plane

body.en:
Scalar Triple Product (Parallelepiped Volume): \[ \mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = \begin{vmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ w_1 & w_2 & w_3 \end{vmatrix}. \] The absolute value \(|\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w})|\) gives the volume of the 3D parallelepiped spanned by \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\).

Plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): Given a point \(P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)\) and a normal vector \(\mathbf{n} = \langle A, B, C \rangle\), the equation of the plane is \[ \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) = 0 \implies A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0. \]

label.en: Level 3 (Advanced Rigor) — Normal Vector, Plane Equation & Triangle Area in 3D

problem.en: Consider three points in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): \(P(1, 0, 2)\), \(Q(2, 3, 1)\), and \(R(0, 1, 4)\). (a) Find the area of \(\triangle PQR\). (b) Find the standard Cartesian equation of the plane passing through \(P, Q, R\).

solution.en:
Step 1: Construct two displacement vectors spanning the plane: \[ \mathbf{u} = \vec{PQ} = \langle 2 - 1, 3 - 0, 1 - 2 \rangle = \langle 1, 3, -1 \rangle, \] \[ \mathbf{v} = \vec{PR} = \langle 0 - 1, 1 - 0, 4 - 2 \rangle = \langle -1, 1, 2 \rangle. \]

Step 2: Compute the normal vector via cross product \(\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\): \[ \mathbf{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(6 - (-1)) - \mathbf{j}(2 - 1) + \mathbf{k}(1 - (-3)) = 7\mathbf{i} - 1\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k} = \langle 7, -1, 4 \rangle. \]

Step 3: Compute triangle area: The area of \(\triangle PQR\) is half the magnitude of the cross product: \[ \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{n}\| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{7^2 + (-1)^2 + 4^2} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{49 + 1 + 16} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{66} \approx 4.062. \]

Step 4: Formulate the plane equation using point \(P(1, 0, 2)\): \[ 7(x - 1) - (y - 0) + 4(z - 2) = 0 \implies 7x - 7 - y + 4z - 8 = 0. \] \[ 7x - y + 4z = 15. \quad \blacksquare \]

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps & Exam Pitfalls — Vectors & Parametric Equations

body.en:
• Scalar vs. Vector Output Distinction: The dot product \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) outputs a pure scalar number, whereas the cross product \(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\) outputs a 3D vector. Never write vector brackets around a dot product!
  • Projection Denominator Mistake: In the vector projection \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2}\mathbf{v}\), the denominator is the squared norm \(\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\), because one factor of \(\|\mathbf{v}\|\) normalizes \(\mathbf{v}\) into a unit vector and the other provides the scalar component. Do not forget the exponent!
  • Cross Product Order (Anti-Commutativity): \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u}\). Reversing the factors reverses the spatial direction: \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = -(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u})\).
  • Parametric Domain Loss in Elimination: When eliminating \(t\) in \(x = e^t, y = e^{2t}\), writing simply \(y = x^2\) is mathematically incorrect without specifying the restricted domain \(x > 0\).

label.en: Worked Example A — Vectors, Lines & Parametric Kinematics (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): Let \( \mathbf{F} = \langle 17, 12 \rangle \) and \( \mathbf{G} = \langle 16, 3 \rangle \) be vectors in \( \mathbb{R}^2 \). Calculate the dot product \( w = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{G} \).

Step-by-Step Solution: The dot product is \( (17)(16) + (12)(3) = 308 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Vectors, Lines & Parametric Kinematics)

rows.en: Vectors are head-to-tail instead of tail-to-tail, giving \(180^\circ - \theta\).
Reverse \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) so both emanate from \(B\): use \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}\).
Using the same parameter \(t\) for two intersecting 3D lines \(\mathbf{r}_1(t) = \mathbf{r}_2(t)\)
Tests for a simultaneous collision at time \(t\) rather than geometric intersection of paths.
Assign distinct parameters \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) to the two lines before equating components.
Multiplying \((AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})\) does not cancel inner factors when \(AB \ne BA\).
Use the shoe-sock reversal law: \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Vectors, Lines & Parametric Kinematics

body.en: Fast Matrix & Vector Verification (Honors Precalculus & Trigonometric Analysis): Check every \(2\times 2\) or \(3\times 3\) eigenvalue computation using the trace and determinant invariants: \(\sum \lambda_i = \operatorname{tr}(A)\) (sum of diagonal entries) and \(\prod \lambda_i = \det(A)\).

question.en: Given vectors \(\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{b} = -3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}\), find the scalar projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\) and the angle \(\theta\) between them to the nearest tenth of a degree.

solution.en:
Calculate the dot product:

\[\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = (2)(-3) + (-5)(4) = -6 - 20 = -26.\]

Calculate the magnitudes:

\[|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 25} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.385,\]\[|\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5.\]

Scalar projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\):

\[\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{-26}{5} = -5.2.\]

Angle \(\theta\) between vectors:

\[\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{-26}{5\sqrt{29}} \approx -0.9656 \implies \theta = \arccos(-0.9656) \approx 164.9°.\]

question.en: Eliminate the parameter to determine the Cartesian equation of the curve \(x = 1 + 2\sec t\), \(y = -2 + 3\tan t\). State the shape, center, and vertices.

solution.en:
Isolate the trigonometric terms:

\[\sec t = \frac{x - 1}{2}, \qquad \tan t = \frac{y + 2}{3}.\]

Apply the fundamental Pythagorean identity \(\sec^2 t - \tan^2 t = 1\):

\[\left(\frac{x - 1}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{y + 2}{3}\right)^2 = 1 \implies \frac{(x - 1)^2}{4} - \frac{(y + 2)^2}{9} = 1.\]

This is a horizontal hyperbola with:

  • Center: \((h, k) = (1, -2)\)
  • Transverse semi-axis: \(a = 2\)
  • Vertices: \((h \pm a, k) = (1 \pm 2, -2) = (-1, -2)\) and \((3, -2)\)
